Six levels of the skill learning sequence. The first three are by ear only and come before reading; *Read it*
and the series section add notation, and the last asks for patterns of your own. Use headphones or speakers, sing and chant out loud, and take a breath before you answer.

The order follows Andy Mullen's: familiar patterns first, then unfamiliar ones. Where Edwin Gordon disagrees, the
note under each section says so.

## Partial synthesis: name the tonality or meter

You hear two series of familiar patterns with **no tonality or meter set up first**. Name the tonality (or meter)
of each. This is still discrimination learning, so the page teaches: after you answer, or when you press
*Tell me*, it explains what to audiate.

<div class="au-panel" id="au-ps"></div>

::: {.au-src}
**Sources.** Gordon: at partial synthesis the teacher does *not* establish tonality or meter, sings the series on
a neutral syllable, and gives the answers; to leave them out would wrongly bridge to generalization-verbal
(*Learning Sequences in Music*, pp. 113, 116; *Reference Handbook*, Tonal Unit 6, pp. 48–49). Both series share one
keyality, so only the resting tone changes. Mullen's objective: "aurally name tonality of a series of familiar
patterns with teacher guidance" (*MLT Any Music Teacher Can Du…De*, p. 74). The meter explanation names the
microbeats you audiate (DU DE or DU DA DI), as Mullen does (p. 85).
:::

## Same or different (generalization-aural/oral)

The tonality or meter is set up, then you hear two patterns, **once each**, and say whether they were the same.
Start with familiar patterns; add unfamiliar ones when that is easy.

<div class="au-panel" id="au-sd"></div>

::: {.au-src}
**Sources.** Gordon: the teacher establishes tonality on a neutral syllable and performs two patterns or sets; at an
inference level the pattern is heard only once, and a student who can't do it goes back to aural/oral
(*Learning Sequences in Music*, pp. 131–132). Gordon uses familiar and unfamiliar patterns here; Mullen starts with
familiar ones, "Ss can identify if patterns are the same or different" right after the aural/oral objectives
(*MLT Any Music Teacher Can Du…De*, pp. 66, 74). Students find *same* easier to hear than *different* (Gordon, p. 219).
:::

## Translate to solfège (generalization-verbal)

You hear the tonality or meter set up, then one pattern on a neutral syllable. **Sing or chant it back in
syllables**, then check. It opens only when the verbal association objective for the same content is done.

<div class="au-panel" id="au-tr"></div>

::: {.au-src}
**Sources.** Gordon warns against this at the verbal association level ("it is not appropriate at this level…");
it belongs to generalization-verbal, where students repeat the teacher's neutral-syllable pattern "using tonal
syllables or rhythm syllables instead" (*Learning Sequences in Music*, pp. 108, 132; *Reference Handbook*, Tonal Unit 9,
Criteria 2–3, pp. 52–54). If students can't, instruction goes back to verbal association; the teacher guides but
does not give the answer first (p. 132). Gordon uses familiar **and unfamiliar** patterns; Mullen practises the
skill with **familiar** patterns first ("students need practice with that skill using familiar patterns before they
try it with unfamiliar patterns", p. 66) and calls it translation (*The Literate Musician*, Rhythm Lessons 8, 9.3,
10.3; Harmony Lesson 9). This page follows Mullen and offers Gordon's unfamiliar patterns as the next step.

**Not checked by the page:** your syllables. You judge them against the answer. Rhythm syllables are the
Gordon/Froseth system: duple DU DE (divisions DU TA DE TA), triple DU DA DI (divisions DU TA DA TA DI TA).
:::

## Read it (symbolic association and generalization-symbolic)

A pattern appears in notation, drawn the way the pattern sets write it: no stems, no rhythm, no syllables. Read it
in syllables, out loud, then hear it and check. Start with **familiar patterns in a new order**; move to
**unfamiliar** ones once you can read the familiar ones yourself. The *name it* choices mix two tonalities or
meters and set neither up first, so you name it from the page.

<div class="au-panel" id="au-gs"></div>

::: {.au-src}
**Sources.** Reading comes after aural/oral, verbal association and partial synthesis, and students first read
patterns they already audiate; tonal patterns are shown on the staff without syllables or rhythm, with DO found from
the DO signature (Gordon, *Learning Sequences in Music*, pp. 117–123). Generalization-symbolic is reading "one
unfamiliar pattern of a mix of familiar and unfamiliar" patterns without the teacher's help and naming the tonality or
meter; if students can't, go back to symbolic association or composite synthesis (pp. 133–134). Mullen: "read
unfamiliar patterns (on the basis of familiar patterns)" (*MLT Any Music Teacher Can Du…De*, p. 39), and reading
familiar patterns in unfamiliar order in a new DO signature (*The Literate Musician*, Reading Lesson 3.1, pp. 122–123).
:::

## Read and write a series (composite synthesis)

Now several familiar patterns at once, and you name the tonality or meter while you read or write them. **Read**: a
series appears; with a *name it* choice nothing is set up, so you name it from the page, then sing or chant it
straight through. **Write from dictation**: hear the series, name it, then write it by choosing each pattern's
notation in order. **Write from memory**: the series shows for three seconds a pattern, then you write it.

<div class="au-panel" id="au-cs"></div>

::: {.au-src}
**Sources.** Composite synthesis joins partial synthesis and symbolic association: students "audiate tonality or meter
of one or more series of familiar tonal patterns or rhythm patterns in familiar or unfamiliar order as they read and
write patterns", and "read with contextual comprehension"; patterns are still read as tonal or rhythm patterns, never
combined into melodic patterns (Gordon, *Learning Sequences in Music*, pp. 126–127). It comes before generalization-symbolic,
and students who struggle there go back to it (pp. 129, 133). Mullen lists the "can do" objectives used here: read a
series of familiar patterns in familiar or unfamiliar order; write a series from dictation; write a series from memory
after seeing it; give the tonality or meter to a series in notation and from dictation (*How to Teach the Language of
Music*, p. 36). **Not the same as real writing:** the page has you choose each pattern's notation from the set rather
than draw it on the staff, so it checks recognition of the notation, not handwriting.
:::

## Answer with your own pattern (creativity/improvisation)

You hear a pattern; answer it out loud with one of your own. *Create* asks only for something different in the same
tonality or meter. *Improvise* adds a rule: the same function, the other function, or (in rhythm) a division. There
is no single right answer: the page can play or list answers from the set that fit, and you judge your own.

<div class="au-panel" id="au-ci"></div>

::: {.au-src}
**Sources.** Creativity sets few restrictions; improvisation adds more, such as function (Gordon, *Learning Sequences
in Music*, p. 136; Mullen, *MLT Any Music Teacher Can Du…De*, pp. 40–41, from exploration through creativity and
improvisation to composition). A tonal answer has as many patterns as the teacher's; a rhythm answer need not
(Gordon, pp. 138–139). Answering on a neutral syllable is creativity/improvisation-aural/oral, which Mullen bridges to
straight after aural/oral; answering in syllables comes after verbal association (Mullen, pp. 66–67, 74). Gordon's
*Reference Handbook* places no restriction on a creative response beyond being tonal, sets function rules for
improvisation, and asks the teacher to be lenient, because bridging to an inference level reinforces the discrimination
level it came from (Tonal Unit 3, pp. 43–45).
:::

## About the patterns and sound

- **Tonal, familiar:** Mullen's familiar patterns in a familiar order (FPIFO), major and minor tonic and dominant,
  15 each (*The Literate Musician*, pp. 57, 59). They are also on [Tonal Patterns](patterns.qmd) as
  *mullen-fpifo-major* and *mullen-fpifo-minor*, with solfège, for verbal association practice.
- **Tonal, unfamiliar:** the site's Register-style sets (*322a*, *322b*, *322b-major*), tonic and dominant only.
- **Dorian and Mixolydian:** the site's tonic/subtonic sets (*323a*, *324a*).
- **Rhythm:** the site's duple (2/4) and triple (6/8) macro/microbeat and division sets, chanted on one pitch.
- Tonality is set with the tonal sequence 5 6 5 4 3 2 7 1 at double speed (Gordon, *Reference Handbook*, p. 33;
  Mullen, p. 79). Meter is set with two bars of microbeats and two of macrobeats; that chant is this site's own.
- Every pitch in a tonal pattern has the same length and every rhythm pattern uses one pitch, as in learning
  sequence activities (Gordon, p. 223). Resting tones stay between D and G above middle C, in the singing range
  Gordon gives (*Reference Handbook*, p. 32).
- The instruments stand in for the neutral syllables "bum" and "bah".
